Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
I've read it. Here's the comment as I understand it, then my assessment. The short version: its corrections are strong, and its conclusion contradicts them.

## Restatement

Varga and Holm re-analyse the Halden microdata and report four problems.

1. **Attrition.** The microdata contradict the working paper. Seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the reduced schedule began. Six of the nine gave workload or output as the reason; only two gave scheduling.
2. **Output.** In the 23 organisations that submitted records, the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index by 3.8 points (98.9 vs 95.1). It was higher in 19 of the 23.
3. **Hours.** Time-tracking data from 27 organisations show actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%. In the 17 organisations with both records and time tracking, the gain in output per actual hour is 10.8%, not 23.4%.
4. **Revenue.** Deflated by 4.1% inflation, the +1.4% becomes about −2.6% in real terms.

They then argue:

- The sector-general claim is an artefact of the metric. Retail fell 11.2% on records, close to Varden's −11.4% for counter offices.
- The remaining 11% is plausibly novelty, based on the energy decline in the survey.
- Varden's meetings finding is a post-hoc subgroup result that should not be cited.
- Per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty".

They recommend record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, longer follow-up and analysis of all enrolled organisations. A data note says the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets, not the whole pilot.

I checked the arithmetic:

- Table 2: 95.1/0.8, 98.4/0.859 and 95.4/0.861 give +18.9%, +14.6% and +10.8%.
- Hours: 40.3 → 34.6 is −14.1%, and 40.4 → 34.8 is −13.9%.
- Real revenue: 1.014/1.041 is −2.6%.

One figure doesn't reconcile; see point 5 below.

## What holds, and matters

Sections 1–5 are good work, and they deserve full weight.

**The attrition finding is the most important new fact in the comment.** If the microdata are right, the working paper misdescribed its own withdrawals. The organisations that dropped out did so after treatment began and mostly because of output problems. That goes beyond a limitation; it is an error in the working paper that the Institute should correct.

**Sections 2 and 3 quantify what was previously only a suspicion.** Earlier I flagged the manager-rated numerator and the scheduled-hours denominator as the two weak inputs to the 23.4%. This comment measures both. Manager ratings run about 4 points high, and actual hours fell by about two-thirds of the scheduled cut. The direction matches Varden, where 22% against scheduled hours became 12.5% against actual hours.

**Sections 4 and 5** are correct. Deflating revenue by CPI is crude, since sector output prices would be better, but the sign of the correction is surely right. On sectors, the record-based retail figure (−11.2%) and Varden's randomised counter result (−11.4%) support each other well, for a 3-organisation subset and a 5-v-5 stratum.

## Where it overshoots

**1. The abstract says attrition was corrected. It wasn't.**
Table 2 corrects output and hours only. Attrition is described in §1 but never quantified. A bound is straightforward:
- Treat the nine withdrawals as enrolled organisations and assign them pessimistic outcomes.
- If they made up roughly 13% of staff and had *zero* per-hour gain, an intention-to-treat version of the 10.8% falls to roughly 9%.
- To erase the gain entirely, the withdrawn organisations would need output well below 80, meaning very large losses.

That is possible, given the stated exit reasons, but it has to be shown. Asserting it isn't enough.

**2. "Entirely an artifact" contradicts the paper's own numbers.**
- After every correction they made, a gain of +10.8% remains.
- The data note says this describes a non-random subset, so the true figure could be higher or lower. That uncertainty cuts both ways; it does not make the estimate zero.
- The conclusion gets to zero only through the novelty argument, which is the weakest section.

**3. The novelty argument rests on self-reported energy, not on output, and the output data are in hand.**
- Energy is the wrong variable for this claim. The Halden output index was collected *monthly*, and the authors have the microdata. If the gain is novelty, output per hour should decline across months one to six, at least in the 17 organisations with records and time tracking. That is the direct test, and it isn't reported.
- The extrapolation is fragile. A straight line through two points (0.61 at month three, 0.29 at month six) reaches zero at about month 8.7, not ten. A straight line is also the wrong shape for a quantity that may level off above zero.
- Varden's 12.5% gain per actual hour was measured at nine months. That is past the point where this extrapolation puts energy back at baseline, and Varden's control offices also knew a trial was running. This doesn't refute novelty, but it is evidence against it, and the comment doesn't engage with it.

"The burden of proof lies with those claiming [durability]" is a reasonable stance for whether the effect lasts. But the honest summary of that stance is "open". It doesn't support "entirely an artifact".

**4. Varden is cited selectively.**
The counter result is called "the most reliable finding in the literature". The case-processing result from the same trial goes unmentioned. That result is randomised, registered, uses records and actual hours, and covers nine months, which are exactly the corrections this comment demands. It found a per-hour gain of 12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4). A conclusion that per-hour gains are entirely artefactual has to deal with that result, and the comment doesn't.

**5. The meetings critique misdescribes what Varden did.**
- The seven offices are not a subgroup "selected for analysis after the results were known". They are the treated arm of a stratum fixed before randomisation.
- The meeting data were collected in month six at managers' request, before results existed. What was unregistered was the analysis, not the selection of offices.
- Varden labelled the finding exploratory, said a seven-office correlation "cannot establish a mechanism", and registered a confirmatory test.

The fair point is narrower: the finding is unconfirmed and shouldn't yet be cited as a mechanism. Varden said the same thing.

**6. The hours breakdown in §3 doesn't add up.**
- The two sources are +0.7 hours a day on four days (+2.8) and 1.6 hours on the day off. Starting from a scheduled 32, that gives about 36.4 hours a week.
- From the baseline day of about 8.06 hours, it gives about 36.6.
- The reported figure is 34.6. Fitting 34.6 would need about +0.2 hours a day.

Either one of the components is wrong or they are measured on different bases. This should be checked against the microdata before the comment is published. It doesn't affect Table 2, which uses the 34.6 figure directly.

## Weighing all three studies together

| Study | Design | Per-hour gain in non-coverage work |
|---|---|---|
| Halden, as published | Uncontrolled | +23.4% (scheduled hours, manager-rated output) |
| Halden, corrected | Uncontrolled, survivors only, non-random subset | +10.8% (records, actual hours) |
| Varden, case-processing | Randomised | +12.5% (records, actual hours) |
| Varden, counter | Randomised | Output per employee −11.4%; Halden retail records −11.2% |

The two studies with independent designs land close together on per-hour gains, at about 11–13%. The coverage-bound results agree too. That agreement is the strongest evidence any of these documents contains, and both the original pilot and this comment miss it.

The evidence supports, at about these weights:

- **Settled for now:** scheduled-hours and manager-rated figures overstate the gain substantially. In presence-bound work run with unchanged opening hours and staffing, output per employee falls by about a tenth.
- **Supported, moderately:** in backlog-type work, output per employee is roughly flat and output per actual hour rises by about an eighth, over at least nine months.
- **Open:** whether that gain persists beyond a year. How much of it comes from cutting meetings rather than from rest. How much attrition-adjusted analysis would shrink it.

The comment ends where the pilot began, but in the opposite direction. The pilot inflated a modest result into "sector-general". The comment deflates the same result into "entirely an artifact". Your first note describes this pair: correcting hard against one error lands on its mirror.

If useful, I can draft a reply to the comment, or a short synthesis note setting out the three-study picture above.
